content: Hyperemia refers to the increased blood flow to various tissues in the body. This phenomenon can have medical implications but also serves as a regulatory response, allowing the adjustment of blood supply to different tissues through the process of vasodilation. When hyperemia occurs in the coronary circulation, it is specifically referred to as TIMI grade 4 flow. Functional hyperemia is characterized by an increase in blood flow to a tissue due to the presence of metabolites and changes in local conditions. When a tissue becomes more active, there is a well-documented decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen and pH, an increase in the partial pressure of carbon dioxide, a rise in temperature, and an elevation in the concentration of potassium ions. Although the exact mechanism of vasodilation remains unclear, it is hypothesized to involve the opening of precapillary sphincters. Active hyperemia is a term used to describe the dilation of arteriolar smooth muscle, which increases blood flow in response to heightened metabolic activity. Reactive hyperemia, on the other hand, refers to a significant increase in blood flow to an organ following a period of occlusion. During this occlusion, there is a shortage of oxygen and an accumulation of metabolic waste products. For example, blood flow to the heart becomes hyperemic when a balloon is inflated in a coronary artery (a case of reactive hyperemia) or in the presence of embolism. This hyperemia in the heart is mediated by the local release of adenosine, which can be measured as it rises in the coronary sinus following embolization.
